questions.question: Describe three causes of hooliganism and explain how each contributes to spectator disorder.

points.text: Three causes: (1) Rivalries - long-standing hatred between clubs (e.g. local derbies) fuels animosity between fan groups, leading to planned confrontations. (2) Alcohol - reduces inhibitions and increases aggression, making intoxicated spectators more likely to engage in violent behaviour. (3) Gang culture - organised firms provide identity and belonging; leaders plan violence through social media

questions.question: Explain how banning orders work and evaluate their effectiveness in reducing hooliganism.

points.text: Banning orders are court-issued legal orders that prevent known hooligans from attending football matches. Individuals must surrender their passports during international tournaments and report to police stations during match times. questions.question: Why are high-risk football matches sometimes given early kick-off times? Explain the reasoning behind this strategy.

points.text: High-risk matches are given early kick-off times (12:30 or 13:30) to reduce the time available for pre-match drinking. When matches kick off early, there is less opportunity for fans to consume large amounts of alcohol in pubs before the game, which reduces the aggression and loss of inhibition associated with intoxication. questions.question: Describe three negative effects of spectator behaviour on sport and suggest how one of these could be addressed.

points.text: Three negative effects: (1) Violence between rival fans endangers safety and can cause serious injury. (2) Property damage to stadiums and surrounding areas costs money and resources. questions.question: Explain how the Taylor Report changed football stadiums in England and why these changes reduced hooliganism.

points.text: The Taylor Report (1990), commissioned after the Hillsborough disaster, recommended that all stadiums in the top two English divisions become all-seater. This eliminated standing terraces where crowd surging could occur and where crowd density was difficult to control.
